title: Capacitors and treble bleeds explained
intro: Understand capacitance, tolerance and the two different jobs a capacitor can do in a guitar.
body:
Tone capacitors

A capacitor’s opposition to alternating current decreases as frequency rises. In a guitar tone branch, the capacitor and tone potentiometer allow higher-frequency signal to reach ground more readily than lower-frequency signal. This is a branch off the signal path, not a component every part of the output must pass through.

As the tone control is rolled down, increasing capacitance generally extends the effect further into lower frequencies. The pickup’s inductance, pot resistance and other loads mean the result is more involved than a single fixed cutoff frequency.

µFnF
0.015µF15nF
0.022µF22nF
0.033µF33nF
0.047µF47nF

These are starting points, not a quality ranking. Compare values with your actual pickups and how far you use the tone control. A value useful on one guitar may be excessive or too subtle on another.

Capacitor construction

Polyester film, polypropylene film and ceramic capacitors use different dielectric materials and constructions. Their specifications can differ in tolerance, stability, temperature behaviour and physical size. A voltage rating describes an operating limit, not an extra amount of “tone”.

Apparition focuses on correct capacitance, appropriate tolerance, measured value, reliable construction and a part that fits the cavity. Brand or price alone is not evidence of an audible benefit. Compare the actual specifications before assuming two capacitors with the same printed value behave differently in your guitar.

What is a treble bleed?

Rolling down a passive guitar’s volume can change the interaction between the pickup, volume pot and cable capacitance, often reducing high-frequency content. A treble bleed provides a frequency-dependent bypass between the volume control’s input and output.

Both Fender and Seymour Duncan describe circuits intended to retain more high-frequency content as volume is reduced. It is an optional response change, not a repair every guitar needs.

Capacitor-only arrangements

The simplest arrangement places a capacitor between volume input and wiper. Apparition’s examples are the 180pF PRS-style Treble Bleed and the 1nF Capacitor-only Treble Bleed. 1nF equals 0.001µF or 1,000pF.

The larger value passes more lower-frequency content through the bypass at a given impedance, but that does not make it better. The effect depends on the pot setting and surrounding circuit. At full volume the input and wiper are already very close electrically, so the bypass has little voltage across it.

View the 180pF example →

Capacitor and resistor in parallel

The 1nF + 150kΩ Duncan-style Treble Bleed connects a capacitor and resistor across the same two volume terminals. Parallel means both component ends share the corresponding input and output connections. The resistor provides a non-frequency-selective path alongside the capacitor and changes the volume control’s effective response and taper.

Do not confuse this with a capacitor and resistor in series. Their electrical behaviour is different. In a two-volume Apparition kit, the chosen bleed configuration is fitted to both volume controls.

View the parallel network →

Which should I choose?

Consider your pickup, pot value, cable capacitance, wiring circuit, volume-control habits and personal preference. If you like the way your guitar loses high end as you reduce volume, you may prefer no treble bleed. If you rely on a clearer reduced-volume sound, a bleed is worth comparing.

Our generator offers standard treble bleeds with Modern and 60s Les Paul wiring. It disables them for its 50s preset, where the tone branch already follows the volume output. This is the supported Apparition configuration, not a claim that every other circuit combination is physically impossible.

Use the links below to compare the actual connections. The diagram explains topology; it does not simulate what your particular guitar will sound like.

Compare: no treble bleed →Compare: capacitor-only →Compare: Duncan-style →Shop capacitors →Shop treble bleeds →

Values and units

1 µF = 1,000 nF = 1,000,000 pF. Common guitar tone values include 0.010, 0.015, 0.022, 0.033 and 0.047 µF, equivalent to 10, 15, 22, 33 and 47 nF. Compare supported values with the tone control position held constant. Tolerance changes the actual capacitance. The voltage rating is a permissible working limit, not a promise of a different guitar response. A large high-voltage part and a small part can have the same capacitance; dielectric, leakage, reliability and physical fit are specifications to consider without assuming an audible benefit from size or brand.

title: Pickup conductors and colour conventions
intro: Separate coil function from wire colour before making a connection.
tags: pickup colours colors conductor coil start finish series link hot shield braided

sections.title: One conductor, two conductors and braid
What these colours do not tell you

body:
One conductor, two conductors and braid

A single insulated core with an outer braid commonly uses the core for signal and the braid as the return and shield. Two insulated conductors can provide separate signal and return, sometimes with an additional shield. Identify your exact construction from the pickup maker’s documentation.

Four conductors and coil ends

A four-conductor humbucker exposes the start and finish of each coil, allowing a normal series connection to be identified. The shared wiring authority names coil functions independently of colour. Coil start and finish are winding references; they do not independently establish magnetic polarity or a complete phase relationship.

Series link, hot and return

In the supported standard series humbucker, two coil ends form the local series link and are insulated together. The remaining signal lead goes to the volume input; the coil return and separate shield terminate at the authorised ground point. The series link is not a ground connection.

Manufacturer colours are conventions

The reference below is rendered from the same pickupConventions registry used by the Generator and Forge. Unresolved profiles show semantic functions rather than invented colours. Check the exact pickup model and manufacturer instructions before relying on a convention.

What these colours do not tell you

Colour mappings do not supply measured pickup resistance, inductance or capacitance. Signal Lab presets are illustrative electrical assumptions. Coil split, phase and series/parallel response modelling are deferred.

title: Selector contacts and pickup paths
intro: A selector connects terminals. Its physical layout must match the circuit you are wiring.
tags: selector 3 way toggle switch common open closed contact
body:
Open and closed contacts

A closed contact provides a conductive path between terminals. An open contact interrupts that path. A selector is a set of these connections, not an electronic mixer with its own gain.

The supported three-way circuit

In the shared Les Paul topology, Neck connects the neck volume output to the common output, Bridge connects the bridge volume output, and Both connects both branches. Circuit Lab shows the actual closed contacts and traces to the jack. Connecting Both physically does not mean Signal Lab has a validated coupled response model.

Identify terminals before soldering

Common means the shared output contact in this context. Switch terminal positions vary by construction. Use the exact switch specification and a continuity test with the guitar disconnected; do not infer terminal function from its location alone.

Use the right tool

Circuit Lab explains paths and contacts. Wiring Generator presents physical destinations. More complex switch topology and coil-level response are not added by this guide.

title: Guitar wiring circuits explained
intro: Follow the signal, understand the controls and compare supported passive wiring.
body:
Start with the signal path

Pickup → Output Jack. A pickup can connect directly to an output, with a hot lead to tip and its return to sleeve. Controls add useful ways to adjust or choose that signal.

Pickup → Volume → Output. A volume control adds a variable signal divider. Pickup → Volume + Tone → Output. The tone network adds a branch to ground; it is not in series with the entire output.

Pickups → Controls → Selector → Output. This describes a traditional Les Paul arrangement. In master-volume circuits such as a Strat or Tele, the selector normally comes before the master volume. There is no single component order for every guitar.

Signal and ground

Hot or signal connections carry the pickup signal towards the output. Ground is the shared return/reference network connected to the jack sleeve. Pickup returns, pot casings, switch frames, shielding and the bridge/string ground belong to this network where specified by the circuit.

A wire crossing another wire in the generator does not make a connection. Only the labelled terminal circles mark junctions. Selecting a wire traces its connected wiring and closed switch contacts, rather than pretending to simulate every current path through resistive components.

Volume and tone

A standard volume uses lug 3 for input, lug 1 for ground and lug 2, the movable wiper, for output. Turn the shaft and the wiper moves along the resistive track. Our rear-view drawings number the downward-facing lugs 3–2–1 from left to right.

The tone pot and capacitor provide a variable frequency-dependent path to ground. The capacitor value sets part of that response; the pot controls the branch resistance. The casing ground and resistive-track terminals are separate connections.

Understand potentiometers →Understand capacitors →

Selector and output jack

A pickup selector connects chosen inputs to an output or other circuit nodes. A blade’s poles are separate switching sections; throws are the contacts selected as the lever moves. A five-way Strat switch can connect adjacent pickup contacts in the in-between positions.

A conventional passive mono output jack uses Tip for signal and Sleeve for common ground. Check with an unplugged cable and a meter to identify the contacts. A contact’s visual position is not enough: jack and switch constructions vary.

Multiple pickups and control arrangements

A master volume adjusts the selected pickup combination. Separate volumes allow individual adjustment, but the wiring matters: in the traditional Les Paul circuit shown here, turning either volume fully down in the Both position also mutes the combined output. “Independent controls” should not be assumed from the number of knobs.

Our classic SSS Strat has a master volume, separate neck and middle tones, and no bridge tone. The Tele preset has master volume and tone. The supported PRS-style superswitch conversion has two humbuckers, master controls and defined split-coil combinations. It is not a universal factory PRS diagram.

View the Strat circuit →View the Tele circuit →View the supported PRS-style circuit →

Modern, 50s and 60s Les Paul wiring

The principal Modern/50s difference is where the tone branch leaves the volume pot. Modern connects it to the input at lug 3. The 50s preset connects it to the output/wiper at lug 2, so the tone network interacts differently as volume changes.

Our 60s preset takes the branch from the volume input and grounds the tone wiper. The generator shows each exact connection, including which tone lug is grounded. These names can be used inconsistently elsewhere; inspect the drawing rather than relying on a label alone. None is universally superior.

View Modern →View 50s →View 60s →

Treble bleeds and coil splitting

A treble bleed belongs across a volume control’s input and output. Its capacitor, sometimes paired with a resistor, changes what passes around the volume track as it is turned down.

A four-conductor humbucker brings out the ends of both coils. Joining two conductors makes the usual series junction. A coil split uses switching to bypass one coil. A partial split places resistance in that bypass so the coil is not shunted as completely. Values and coil choices depend on the verified circuit; do not copy them by colour from a different pickup brand.

A split humbucker generally loses its normal hum-cancelling operation. “Coil tap” is a different construction feature and is not another name for coil splitting.

Read about treble bleeds →

Series, parallel and phase

Series connects components end-to-end; parallel connects them across shared nodes. Two humbucker coils are commonly in series internally, while two selected guitar pickups are commonly combined in parallel. Changing these arrangements changes the combined impedance and output.

Phase reversal changes one pickup’s electrical polarity relative to another and is mainly heard when they are combined. It is not the same as selecting a different coil. Keep a separate shield grounded; do not repurpose a grounded cover or bare shield as a hot connection.

Advanced switching must match the available conductors and switch contacts. Unsupported modifications remain unavailable until their circuit is checked.

title: Ground, shield and the output jack
intro: Follow the signal return and keep shielding roles clear.
tags: ground hum noise shield drain bridge strings sleeve tip output jack continuity

sections.title: Ground is a node; shielding is a role

body:
Signal ground and output

Signal ground is the circuit’s reference and return path. The output jack sleeve connects to that return; the tip carries the output signal. Identify tip and sleeve contacts on the actual jack, rather than using their apparent position.

Pot casings and shared return

The supported wiring uses authorised casing solder points and a shared ground harness. A grounded lug is a separate electrical connection from the metal casing. Check each required bond and the final sleeve connection.

Ground is a node; shielding is a role

A shield or drain conductor can connect to the ground reference while its purpose is to reduce interference reaching the signal wiring. Coil return and shield are separately identified even when they terminate at one casing point. A shield is not an interchangeable signal lead.

Bridge and string ground

Where the instrument design requires it, the bridge/string bond connects the metal hardware to the guitar’s ground network. Touching grounded strings can change picked-up interference; it does not by itself prove the entire wiring is correct.

Check continuity safely

Disconnect the guitar from the amplifier before resistance or continuity checks. Compare the intended ground points with jack sleeve, and inspect for loose joints or shorts to hot terminals. A continuity reading alone does not diagnose every intermittent fault. This guide concerns passive guitars; do not open mains-powered amplifier equipment.

title: Wire a Les Paul using your kit
intro: Prepare, connect, inspect and test against the diagram for your supported configuration.
tags: solder installation wiring kit bench continuity
body:
Before you start

Soldering equipment becomes extremely hot. Work on a heat-resistant surface with ventilation and eye protection, keep the iron in its stand and protect the guitar finish. Disconnect the guitar from the amplifier and any power source. Only undertake work you are comfortable performing; ask a qualified guitar technician if you are unsure.

Photograph the original wiring from several angles and label each wire before removing anything. Identify the pickups and their exact conductor convention. Confirm shaft/bushing length, diameter, knob fit, cavity depth and control spacing. A Les Paul-style model name alone does not confirm compatibility.

Prepare a clean, well-lit workspace and a padded support that does not react with the finish. Keep solder and hot tools away from the instrument surface. This guide covers the supported passive harness; active pickups and additional switching need their own instructions.

Tools

  • Temperature-controlled soldering iron and appropriate electronics solder
  • Wire cutters, suitable wire strippers and small pliers
  • Nut drivers or spanners matching the hardware
  • Multimeter and a known-good guitar cable
  • Heat-resistant working surface, suitable finish protection and ventilation

Use tools sized for the job. Do not use acid-core plumbing solder. Set up the iron according to the tool, solder and component guidance; excessive heating can damage pots, insulation and the guitar finish.

Step 1 / Identify the circuit

No saved kit has been opened with this guide. Configure your kit or choose the matching circuit before soldering.

Open your selected diagram and check wiring style, capacitor values, treble bleeds and supplied hardware. The diagram includes existing pickups, grounds and any jack or selector you are retaining. “Existing / Not included” means electrically required but not newly supplied.

Open your wiring diagram →

Step 2 / Remove the existing controls

Loosen or remove strings only as needed for safe access. Remove cavity covers or other access parts carefully and retain screws. Identify every connection before desoldering it, and preserve sufficient usable lead length. Support a potentiometer or jack while loosening its nut so it cannot twist and pull wires.

Construction differs between guitars. Do not assume a control can pass through an opening or that a connector, mounting hole or cavity is compatible. Stop if removal requires unexpected force.

Step 3 / Install the potentiometers

Test the harness fit before soldering the external connections. Orient the pots so terminals and capacitors have clearance from cavity walls, shielding and covers. Use the appropriate washers and nuts, support each component and tighten only enough to secure it. Avoid twisting the assembled harness.

Do not force shafts or incompatible knobs, overtighten mounting nuts or bend capacitor leads sharply at the body. Check that the control cavity closes without pressing on components.

Step 4 / Connect pickups

Follow the generated pickup-hot and ground connections. Verify your exact manufacturer/model wiring convention before soldering. The Generator’s colour selector identifies which conventions are verified; an unverified choice uses functional generic labels, not guessed colours.

For a standard series humbucker, join and insulate the designated series-link wires as shown. Keep the bare shield on ground. A braided two-conductor pickup does not provide separate access to both coil ends and cannot be treated as a four-conductor pickup for splitting.

Step 5 / Connect the selector

Identify the neck input, bridge input, output contacts and frame ground on the actual switch using its documentation and a continuity meter. Follow the generated diagram, including the joined output contacts where shown. Similar-looking switches may have different terminal arrangements.

If no new selector was ordered, reconnect the existing one to the required circuit destinations. Keep signal connections insulated from the switch frame and nearby shielding.

Step 6 / Connect the output jack

Connect the output signal to Tip and common ground to Sleeve in the supported passive mono circuit. Use a known-good unplugged cable and continuity checks to identify the corresponding contacts. Some multi-contact jacks use several spring contacts for the same electrical node; follow the selected part’s documentation.

Secure the jack without allowing it to rotate and strain the wires. Check that an inserted plug does not touch a signal lug or trap a wire against shielding.

Step 7 / Grounding

Retain the bridge/string ground and connect it to the common ground network shown. Confirm continuity between jack sleeve, specified pot casings, pickup shields, switch frame and bridge/string ground. Shielding, where fitted, must not touch hot terminals.

Do not remove a bridge ground simply to hide a noise problem, and do not modify amplifier mains wiring. Unexplained noise or an unfamiliar grounding arrangement warrants further diagnosis.

Step 8 / Inspect before testing

Check each connection against the drawing. Look for loose or incompletely wetted solder joints, stray wire strands, bridges between adjacent lugs, melted insulation and unwanted contact with shielding. Check ground wires and every component terminal, including places hidden underneath the harness.

Let joints cool before moving them. A large solder blob does not guarantee a reliable connection. Resolve mechanical strain and exposed conductors before electrical testing.

Step 9 / Electrical test

With the instrument disconnected from the amplifier, check intended ground continuity and selector operation. At full volume, check for an unintended near-zero resistance between jack tip and sleeve. A pickup circuit normally presents a finite DC resistance, while a volume at zero intentionally grounds the output; do not interpret every continuity beep as a fault.

Check the resistance changes as each volume is moved and compare selector readings logically. Capacitors do not pass steady DC, so a meter’s resistance or continuity setting cannot confirm a complete tone-control response. Check component values out of circuit where parallel paths would affect the reading.

Step 10 / Functional test

After the basic checks pass, connect to a known-good amplifier at low volume. Confirm neck, bridge and both selector positions; check both volume and tone controls over their full travel. Check for intermittent connections as you gently operate controls, without pulling the wiring.

Play the guitar to assess any treble bleed as volume is reduced. Check additional switching only against its specific verified instructions. The standard Les Paul circuit mutes both pickups when either volume is at zero in the Both position; that is expected for this wiring.

Only refit covers once everything works, ensuring no wires or components are pinched. Retest after final assembly.

title: Passive guitar troubleshooting
intro: Start with a symptom, narrow the checks, and inspect the appropriate circuit view.
tags: hum crackle no output mute intermittent selector problem diagnosis
body:
Symptoms suggest areas to inspect; they do not prove a diagnosis. Disconnect the guitar before continuity tests. Keep amplifier checks external; never work on mains-powered amplifier internals.

No output

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Check the cable and amplifier input with a known working guitar first, then jack tip/sleeve wiring, unwanted hot-to-ground shorts and selector output.

Learn: Ground, shield and the output jack → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

One pickup does not work

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Compare both single-pickup positions. Inspect its hot lead, return, series link and selector branch against the diagram.

Learn: Pickup conductors and colour conventions → · Inspect: Signal Forge / Circuit Lab →

Volume does not fully mute

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Check the ground-end lug bond and the input/wiper identification against the selected wiring. Do not assume every two-volume topology behaves identically.

Learn: Potentiometers explained → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

Tone control does nothing

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Inspect the capacitor connection, tone wiper and required ground bond. Check the selected wiring style before moving a lead.

Learn: Capacitors and treble bleeds explained → · Inspect: Signal Forge / Signal Lab →

Hum changes when touching strings

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Inspect bridge/string ground and shielding continuity. This symptom can be consistent with interference pickup but is not proof of a specific fault.

Learn: Ground, shield and the output jack → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

Hum does not change when touching strings

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Try another cable and environment, then inspect shielding, return paths and pickup type. Single-coil interference is not always a wiring defect.

Learn: Ground, shield and the output jack → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

Crackling pot

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Check whether movement of the shaft or a nearby lead reproduces it. Inspect joints and the control; use only suitable contact maintenance for the part.

Learn: Potentiometers explained → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

Intermittent output

Likely areas and safe basic checks

With the guitar disconnected, inspect loose jack contacts, fractured joints and leads that move or short. Avoid pulling delicate pickup wires.

Learn: Ground, shield and the output jack → · Inspect: Wiring Generator →

Selector position not working

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Identify the actual common and contact pairs with a disconnected continuity test. Compare the expected path in Circuit Lab.

Learn: Selector contacts and pickup paths → · Inspect: Signal Forge / Circuit Lab →

Treble bleed behaves strangely

Likely areas and safe basic checks

Verify input/wiper terminals and whether the resistor is parallel or series. Compare the pot, cable/load and volume assumptions in the Designer.

Learn: Choosing a treble bleed in context → · Inspect: Treble Bleed Designer →

title: Guitar electronics glossary
intro: Concise definitions of the terms used in Apparition’s guides and tools.
tags: wiper lug common sleeve capacitance resistance taper load terminology
body:
Capacitance
Ability to store charge per voltage difference; measured in farads. Guitar values commonly use µF, nF and pF. Learn more →
Resistance
Opposition to current in a resistive path; measured in ohms (Ω). Learn more →
Potentiometer
A resistive track with two ends and a movable wiper. Learn more →
Audio / log taper
A non-linear relationship between rotation and wiper resistance, commonly used for volume controls. Exact laws vary. Learn more →
Linear taper
A nominally linear relationship between rotation and wiper resistance. Learn more →
Wiper
The moving contact on a potentiometer track. Learn more →
Lug
A physical terminal for making an electrical connection. Learn more →
Ground
The circuit reference and return node; not automatically mains protective earth. Learn more →
Shield
A conductive screen intended to reduce interference coupling into signal wiring. Learn more →
Hot
The signal-bearing conductor or node relative to the circuit return. Learn more →
Series
Components connected consecutively so the same branch current passes through them. Learn more →
Parallel
Branches connected across the same two electrical nodes. Learn more →
Treble bleed
A network between a volume input and wiper that changes reduced-volume frequency response. Learn more →
Tone capacitor
A capacitor in the tone branch that contributes frequency-dependent impedance. Learn more →
Pickup conductor
A lead connected to a coil end or shield; its colour follows a convention. Learn more →
Coil start
One winding end identified as the start in a documented convention. Learn more →
Coil finish
The other winding end identified as the finish; electrical phase also depends on winding and magnetic orientation. Learn more →
Series link
The local connection between two coil ends in a series humbucker. Learn more →
Selector contact
A conductive switch surface that connects or disconnects terminals. Learn more →
Common
A shared selector output contact in the supported pickup circuit. Learn more →
Tip
The signal contact of the supported mono output jack. Learn more →
Sleeve
The return contact of the supported mono output jack. Learn more →
Load
The impedance presented to a source by the rest of the circuit. Learn more →
Input resistance
The resistive part of the external input load represented in the model. Learn more →
Cable capacitance
The cable’s capacitance between signal and return, included as a load assumption. Learn more →
